## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Rukkhadhammajātaka* (Ja 74) is a short narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary (*Jātakatthavaṇṇanā*), the Buddha delivered the teaching while residing at Jetavana to settle a fierce water dispute among his kinsfolk along the Rohiṇī river [SuttaCentral; Appleton; Fausböll 1877]. Travelling through the air, the Buddha sat above the river emitting dark rays to shock his relatives into composure, then descended to the riverbank to exhort them to live in unity and concord, referencing the full account given in the *Kuṇāla-jātaka* and beginning with the verse *sādhu sambahulā ñātīti* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was born as a tree-deity dwelling in a sāla tree in the Himalayas [SuttaCentral; Appleton; Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009]. He instructed the other tree-deities to establish their dwellings close to one another and near him in the forest; however, some deities, seeking rich offerings from human villages, chose isolated solitary trees instead [Appleton]. When a powerful tempest struck the region, the interlaced trees, shrubs, and bushes of the forest sheltered one another and remained standing, while the solitary trees were uprooted and destroyed, driving the disobedient deities back to the safety of the forest [SuttaCentral; Appleton; Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009]. Scholars have highlighted this Jātaka as an ethical instruction utilizing observations of the natural world to teach social cohesion, familial solidarity, and the mutual protection afforded by unity [Storhoff and Whalen-Bridge 2010; Saddhatissa 1997; Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009].
SuttaCentral records no cross-language parallels for this discourse [SuttaCentral]. Similarly, DharmaNexus detects no Pali-internal text reuse and finds no cross-language matches with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora meeting its threshold [DharmaNexus].
